He wants to escape from Scotland by sea at once

questions.text: In Act 1 Scene 7, how does Lady Macbeth persuade Macbeth to go ahead with the murder of Duncan?

rubric.model_answer: Lady Macbeth attacks Macbeth's manhood: 'When you durst do it, then you were a man', so the murder becomes a test of masculinity. She calls him a coward and claims she would do something terrible rather than break a promise as he has, which shames him. She commands him to 'screw your courage to the sticking-place' and then gives a practical plan: drug the guards and blame them. Her mix of insults, commands and a clear plan overcomes his doubts.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: clear point about how she persuades him (e.g. questioning his manhood)
1 mark: relevant quotation from Act 1 Scene 7
1 mark: analysis of her language (insults, imperatives, questions)
1 mark: explains the effect (Macbeth changes his mind and agrees)

questions.solution: Key ideas: she questions his manhood, calls him a coward, uses commands and gives him a practical plan
questions.hint: Look at what Lady Macbeth says about being 'a man'

questions.text: Which statement about the Jacobean context of Macbeth is accurate?

The play was written to celebrate Queen Elizabeth I's coronation

questions.text: Killing a king was seen as an especially terrible crime in Shakespeare's time. Why?

options: Kings were elected by Parliament for a single year
Kings were believed to be chosen by God (Divine Right)
Kings were believed to be immortal and unable to die
Only witches were allowed to choose new kings

questions.solution: Under the Divine Right of Kings, killing a king was a crime against God and the natural order
questions.hint: Think about where Jacobeans believed a king's power came from

questions.text: In Act 2 Scene 4, Ross and an Old Man describe darkness in the daytime and Duncan's horses eating each other. What do these details suggest?

options: Scotland is simply having an ordinary, stormy winter
The witches have started a war between Scotland and England
Killing the king has disturbed the natural order
Duncan's horses were badly trained and hungry

questions.solution: These unnatural events mirror the unnatural crime of killing a king, which upsets God's order
questions.hint: Jacobeans believed the king sat near the top of a God-given order

questions.text: Macbeth's 'Life's but a walking shadow' speech comes just after he hears of his wife's death. What does the speech mainly show?

options: His relief at finally being free
His plan to win the battle using magic
His joy at becoming king
His despair: life now seems meaningless to him

questions.solution: He calls life a tale 'Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, / Signifying nothing', showing utter despair
questions.hint: What does a 'shadow' suggest about how real or important life is?

questions.text: Give the term for the murder of a king, the crime at the centre of the play.
questions.solution: Regicide means killing a king: Macbeth's murder of Duncan
questions.hint: It ends in -cide, like 'homicide'

questions.text: 'Macbeth is a tragic hero, not simply a villain.' How far do you agree?

rubric.model_answer: Macbeth begins as 'brave Macbeth', a loyal soldier praised by Duncan, so he has the high status of a tragic hero. His fatal flaw, 'vaulting ambition', leads him to murder, yet his guilt ('Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood') shows a conscience a simple villain would lack. However, he later orders the killing of Macduff's family without hesitation, which seems villainous. By the end, his despair in 'Life's but a walking shadow' makes the audience feel pity as well as horror.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: clear argument that answers 'how far'
1 mark: Macbeth's noble start (e.g. 'brave Macbeth')
1 mark: his fatal flaw (ambition) and its results
1 mark: evidence of guilt or conscience
1 mark: his villainous acts considered (e.g. Macduff's family)
1 mark: tragic structure or audience response (pity and fear)

questions.solution: A balanced answer weighs his noble start, ambition, guilt and later cruelty, and the pity he provokes at the end
questions.hint: List what makes him admirable at the start, then what he does later

questions.text: In Stave 1, how does Dickens use cold weather and coldness to present Scrooge?

rubric.model_answer: Dickens links Scrooge with cold to show he is unfeeling. 'The cold within him froze his old features', suggesting his meanness comes from inside and even shapes how he looks. Dickens adds 'No warmth could warm, no wintry weather chill him', implying he is colder than winter itself. Scrooge keeps Bob's fire tiny, so his coldness makes others suffer. This prepares for the warmth of his change in Stave 5.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: clear point linking coldness to Scrooge's character
1 mark: relevant quotation from Stave 1
1 mark: analysis of language (e.g. 'cold within him', 'froze')
1 mark: effect on others or link to his later change

questions.solution: Key ideas: coldness inside Scrooge, Dickens's cold imagery, Bob's tiny fire and the contrast with his later warmth
questions.hint: Find where Dickens describes Scrooge's appearance and his office fire

questions.text: Which statement about the context of A Christmas Carol is accurate?

questions.text: Scrooge's phrase 'decrease the surplus population' echoes the ideas of an economist who wrote about population growth. Give his surname.

questions.text: How does Dickens use the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come to complete Scrooge's change?

rubric.model_answer: The silent, hooded Phantom frightens Scrooge more than any other spirit, and its silence forces him to work out the meaning of each scene himself. He sees businessmen joke about a dead man, people sell the man's belongings at Old Joe's, and the Cratchits grieving for Tiny Tim. Finally he sees his own neglected grave. These visions show that a selfish life ends unloved and that his choices affect others, so he begs for the chance to change. Dickens uses this fear to make his message urgent.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: clear argument about the Ghost's role in Scrooge's change
1 mark: the Ghost's silence and appearance and their effect
1 mark: the reactions to the dead man (businessmen, Old Joe's)
1 mark: the Cratchits' grief for Tiny Tim
1 mark: the gravestone and Scrooge's plea to change
1 mark: Dickens's purpose or message for readers

questions.solution: Key ideas: the frightening silence, the unloved dead man, Tiny Tim's death, the gravestone and Scrooge's plea to change
questions.hint: Think about each scene the Phantom shows, and how Scrooge reacts

questions.text: Why did Priestley set the play in 1912 but write it for an audience in 1945?

options: So the audience could see how wrong Birling's predictions were
Because the law required all plays to be set in the past
Because he knew nothing about events after 1912
To make the costumes and the set cheaper to produce

questions.text: How do Sheila and Eric differ from their parents by the end of the play?

The children accept responsibility; the parents mostly do not

News that Gerald has been arrested by the police

News that Mr Birling has been given his knighthood

questions.text: Which description of the play's structure is accurate?

options: Five acts set over several years
Many short scenes in different cities

questions.text: How does Priestley use the opening of Act 1, before the Inspector arrives, to present the Birlings?

rubric.model_answer: Priestley's stage directions describe a large, comfortable dining room and soft, warm lighting, suggesting a wealthy, self-satisfied family. Mr Birling dominates the conversation, boasting about his business, his link to the Crofts and his hopes of a knighthood. He confidently claims the Titanic cannot sink and that war will not happen, which the 1945 audience knew was wrong. This dramatic irony makes him look foolish, so the audience distrusts his selfish views before the Inspector even arrives.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: comment on the setting or lighting and what it suggests
1 mark: Mr Birling's boasting or self-importance
1 mark: dramatic irony (Titanic, war) and its effect
1 mark: how the audience is led to judge the family

questions.solution: Key ideas: a comfortable, wealthy setting, Birling's boasting and wrong predictions, and dramatic irony
questions.hint: Think about the setting, the lighting and what Mr Birling talks about

options: To arrest Eric for stealing from his father's firm
To voice Priestley's message of social responsibility
To provide comic relief in a serious, tense play
To make sure Mr Birling gets his knighthood

questions.solution: The Inspector drives the plot and voices Priestley's message of social responsibility

questions.text: After Gerald learns there is no Inspector Goole in the local police, how do Mr and Mrs Birling react?

options: They confess everything to the newspapers
They give all their money to charity

questions.text: Why is Eva Smith important in the play beyond being a single character?

She is the Inspector's daughter in disguise

questions.solution: Her very common name suggests she stands for countless working-class people

questions.text: Which theme, beginning with R, does the Inspector want every member of the family to accept? Give the one-word theme.
questions.solution: Responsibility: the Inspector shows that each Birling played a part in Eva's fate

questions.text: How does Priestley use the ending of the play to make the audience think about responsibility?

rubric.model_answer: After the Inspector leaves, the family splits. Sheila and Eric still feel responsible, but Mr and Mrs Birling and Gerald celebrate when it seems there was no real inspector and no recent death. Priestley then has the phone ring with news of a young woman's death and a real inspector coming to question them. This twist denies the older characters an easy escape and suggests their actions will be judged. The audience is left questioning who the Inspector was and pushed to accept that everyone shares responsibility for others.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: clear argument about the purpose of the ending
1 mark: the split between the generations
1 mark: the relief of Mr and Mrs Birling and Gerald
1 mark: the final phone call and its effect
1 mark: the mystery of the Inspector's identity
1 mark: link to Priestley's message or 1945 context

questions.solution: Key ideas: the generational split, the older characters' relief, the final phone call and Priestley's message about shared responsibility
questions.hint: Think about who has changed by the end, and what the final phone call means

questions.text: How does Blake present suffering in 'London'?

rubric.model_answer: Blake presents suffering as everywhere. The repetition in 'In every cry of every Man' suggests no one escapes it. He blames those in power: the 'charter'd' streets suggest that even the city is owned and controlled. The 'mind-forg'd manacles' imply people are trapped by oppression and by their own thinking. The 'hapless Soldier's sigh' that 'Runs in blood down Palace walls' links the suffering of ordinary soldiers to the monarchy.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: clear point about how suffering is presented
1 mark: relevant quotation from the poem
1 mark: analysis of language or repetition (e.g. 'every', 'charter'd', 'manacles')
1 mark: link to who Blake blames (those in power, church, monarchy)

questions.solution: Key ideas: suffering is everywhere ('every'), control by the powerful ('charter'd') and people trapped ('mind-forg'd manacles')
questions.hint: Look at the words Blake repeats and who he blames

As a beautiful backdrop for a love story

questions.text: In 'Exposure', Owen pairs words such as 'silent' and 'salient', which share their consonants but have different vowel sounds. Give the term for this kind of rhyme.

questions.text: Compare how Owen in 'Exposure' and Tennyson in 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' present soldiers' experience of war.

rubric.model_answer: Tennyson presents soldiers as heroic: the 'Noble six hundred' obey without question ('Theirs not to reason why'), and the galloping dactylic rhythm creates excitement. Owen, a soldier himself, presents war as slow, miserable waiting: the refrain 'But nothing happens' stresses boredom, and the weather is the real enemy ('merciless iced east winds that knive us'). Tennyson glorifies sacrifice from newspaper reports, while Owen's first-hand experience exposes suffering and pointlessness.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: clear comparison of the two poems' views of war
1 mark: Tennyson's heroic presentation with a quotation
1 mark: Owen's presentation of suffering or waiting with a quotation
1 mark: comparison of form or structure (rhythm, refrain)
1 mark: context (newspaper report versus first-hand experience)
1 mark: comparative connectives used throughout

questions.solution: Key ideas: Tennyson's heroic, fast-paced glory against Owen's slow, freezing suffering; second-hand versus first-hand experience
questions.hint: Start with one big difference: who is the real enemy in each poem?

questions.text: How does Shakespeare present Mercutio in Act 3 Scene 1?

rubric.model_answer: Mercutio is presented as witty and fiery. He provokes Tybalt and fights him when Romeo refuses, showing his loyalty and quick temper. Even when dying he jokes: 'ask for me tomorrow, and you shall find me a grave man', a pun that shows his wit. His curse, 'A plague o' both your houses!', blames both families for the feud and foreshadows the tragedy to come. His death is the turning point that drives Romeo to kill Tybalt.

questions.text: How does Shakespeare present the conflict between love and hate in Act 1 Scene 5?

rubric.model_answer: In Act 1 Scene 5 love and hate are placed side by side. Romeo's wonder at Juliet ('O, she doth teach the torches to burn bright!') uses light imagery to show sudden, intense love. At the same moment Tybalt recognises Romeo and wants to fight, so the audience sees hatred threatening the lovers. Their shared sonnet presents love as perfect and holy, yet Juliet's line 'My only love sprung from my only hate!' shows their love is born inside the feud, foreshadowing tragedy.

1 mark: Juliet's 'only love... only hate' and its antithesis
1 mark: link to fate, foreshadowing or the Prologue

questions.solution: Key ideas: light imagery of love, Tybalt's hatred in the same scene, the shared sonnet and Juliet's 'only love... only hate'
questions.hint: Track what Romeo says, what Tybalt does, and what Juliet realises

options: Guest
Enfield
Newcomen
Poole
feedback: Mr Guest is Utterson's head clerk
Enfield is Utterson's relative and walking companion
Newcomen is the police inspector

questions.text: In which year was Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde first published? Give the year.
questions.solution: It was published in January 1886
questions.hint: It was in the mid-1880s

questions.text: Name the doctor, Jekyll's old friend, who dies after seeing Hyde transform. Give the name.
questions.solution: Dr Hastie Lanyon is so shocked by what he sees that he dies soon afterwards
questions.hint: He had quarrelled with Jekyll about science years before

questions.text: In the first chapter, what does Hyde do that shocks Enfield?

options: He tramples over a young girl in the street
He robs a bank in the middle of the night
He attacks Sir Danvers Carew with a cane
He sets fire to a house on a quiet street
feedback: That happens later, in 'The Carew Murder Case'

questions.solution: Hyde tramples a girl at about three in the morning, then pays her family with a cheque in Jekyll's name
questions.hint: It happens in the street at about three in the morning

questions.text: Which Member of Parliament does Hyde murder?

options: Dr Lanyon
Sir Danvers Carew
Mr Enfield
Poole
feedback: Lanyon dies of shock, not murder

questions.solution: Hyde attacks Sir Danvers Carew, an MP, in a street, and a maid sees it from her window
questions.hint: A maid sees the attack from her window

questions.text: Whose narrative describes actually watching Hyde turn into Jekyll?

options: Mr Enfield's
Poole's
Dr Lanyon's
Mr Guest's

questions.solution: In 'Dr Lanyon's Narrative', Lanyon watches Hyde drink the potion and become Jekyll
questions.hint: This witness dies soon afterwards from the shock

questions.text: What does Jekyll's will say should happen if he dies or disappears?

options: Everything goes to Utterson
Everything goes to charity
His house goes to Poole
Everything goes to Edward Hyde

questions.solution: The will leaves everything to Hyde, which alarms Utterson
questions.hint: The will worries Utterson because of who benefits

questions.text: What is Mr Hyde's first name? Give the name.
questions.solution: Edward Hyde; Jekyll's first name is Henry
questions.hint: It is also the name of several English kings

questions.text: Who is Utterson's distant relative who tells the 'Story of the Door'? Give the name.
questions.solution: Richard Enfield, Utterson's distant relative and walking companion
questions.hint: He walks with Utterson every Sunday

questions.text: Half of a broken walking stick is found where Carew was attacked. Why does Utterson recognise it?

options: He had given it to Jekyll years before
It belongs to Poole
He saw Hyde buy it in Soho
It was taken from his own office that morning

questions.solution: Utterson had given the stick to Jekyll, which links Hyde to Jekyll
questions.hint: Think about who Utterson once gave a present to

questions.text: How do people react when they see Hyde?

options: They find him handsome, charming and polite
They feel instant disgust but cannot say why
They think he looks exactly like Dr Jekyll
They hardly notice him at all in the street

questions.solution: Everyone who meets Hyde feels loathing but cannot name a clear deformity
questions.hint: Enfield struggles to describe what is wrong with Hyde's appearance

questions.text: Mr Guest, Utterson's clerk, compares a note from Jekyll with a letter signed by Hyde. What does he notice?

options: One note is written in French and the other in English
Neither of the two documents has a signature at the end
The handwriting is almost identical, only sloped differently
Hyde's letter is written in pencil rather than in ink

questions.solution: Guest sees that the two hands are nearly identical, only differently sloped: Jekyll has written for Hyde
questions.hint: Guest is an expert in handwriting

questions.text: In 'Incident at the Window', what do Utterson and Enfield see?

options: Hyde climbing out of the window into the yard
Lanyon waving at them from a passing carriage
Poole arguing angrily with Hyde at the door
Jekyll at a window, suddenly looking terrified

questions.solution: Jekyll's look of 'abject terror and despair' horrifies them
questions.hint: They are in the courtyard and see their friend above them

questions.text: Utterson thinks: 'If he be Mr Hyde, I shall be Mr ___.' Give the missing word.
questions.solution: 'Mr Seek': Utterson puns on hide-and-seek, showing his determination to find Hyde
questions.hint: Think of a children's game in which one player hides

questions.text: In which district of London does Hyde have his house? Give the name.
questions.solution: Hyde lives in Soho, which had a poor and disreputable reputation at the time
questions.hint: It is in the West End and begins with S

questions.text: Stevenson often describes London in thick fog. What does the fog suggest?

options: Secrecy and mystery, as the truth is hidden
That it is a hot, bright day in midsummer
That London is a clean and modern city
That Hyde works as a sailor on the river

questions.solution: The fog hides things, mirroring the secrets of Jekyll and of respectable society
questions.hint: What does fog do to what you can see?

questions.text: Why is Utterson reluctant to expose Jekyll's secret?

options: He is secretly working with Hyde for money
He wants to protect his friend's reputation
He is too ill to leave his house in London
He does not know Jekyll well enough to care

questions.solution: Victorian gentlemen valued reputation, and Utterson fears a scandal for his friend
questions.hint: Think about what mattered most to a Victorian gentleman

questions.text: In Jekyll's full statement, why did he first make the potion?

options: To cure his friend Lanyon of a serious illness
To make himself invisible so he could spy on people
To separate the good and evil sides of his nature
To make himself rich by selling the medicine

questions.solution: He hoped to separate his two natures so that each could live without the other's restraint
questions.hint: He believed every person has two sides

questions.text: Why does Jekyll lose control of the transformations near the end?

options: Poole hides the potion and refuses to give it back
Utterson destroys his laboratory to protect him
Lanyon steals his notes and the recipe for the potion
He transforms without the potion, and his special salt runs out

questions.solution: Hyde appears without the drug, and the original salt had an unknown impurity that could not be replaced
questions.hint: Something was special about the first batch of salt

questions.text: Give the one-word term for the idea that a person has both a good and an evil side, a central theme of the novella.
questions.solution: Duality: Jekyll writes that man is 'not truly one, but truly two'
questions.hint: It comes from the Latin for 'two'

questions.text: How does Stevenson present Mr Utterson in the first chapter?

rubric.model_answer: Stevenson presents Utterson as a reserved but loyal gentleman. He is described as 'lean, long, dusty, dreary' and yet 'somehow lovable', suggesting a dull surface that hides warmth. He is self-disciplined, drinking gin when alone to curb his taste for fine wine. His saying 'I incline to Cain's heresy' shows he does not judge others, which makes him a trustworthy guide for the reader, while his care for reputation reflects Victorian values.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: clear point about Utterson's character
1 mark: relevant quotation from the first chapter
1 mark: analysis of language (e.g. 'dusty, dreary', 'somehow lovable')
1 mark: link to his role in the novella or Victorian values

questions.solution: Key ideas: dull and reserved on the surface but loyal and lovable, self-disciplined, tolerant and concerned with reputation
questions.hint: Look at how Stevenson describes Utterson in the first paragraph

questions.text: Which statement about the context of the novella is accurate?

options: Victorian gentlemen were expected to keep a respectable public reputation
Victorian society encouraged people to share their secrets openly
The novella was written after the First World War
Stevenson wrote it to celebrate science without question

questions.solution: Respectability mattered greatly, so Jekyll hides his desires and creates Hyde
questions.hint: Why can't Jekyll simply behave badly as himself?

questions.text: Hyde is described as 'ape-like'. Which Victorian fear does this reflect?

options: That apes were escaping from London Zoo at night
That humans might slide back into a primitive, animal state
That electricity would make cities too dangerous
That machines would soon replace all workers

questions.solution: After theories of evolution, some Victorians feared humans could degenerate into a primitive state
questions.hint: Think about debates on evolution in the later 1800s

questions.text: Why does Stevenson tell most of the story through Utterson rather than Jekyll?

options: Because Utterson is secretly the villain of the story
Because Jekyll is too busy to write his own story
So the reader shares his confusion and the mystery lasts
So the ending can be revealed in the first chapter

questions.solution: Following Utterson, we only learn the truth from the documents at the end
questions.hint: When does the reader learn that Jekyll and Hyde are the same man?

questions.text: Which statement about the structure of the novella is accurate?

options: It is told entirely in letters between Jekyll and Hyde
It opens with Jekyll's full confession of his crimes
It is a play in five acts set in a single room
It ends with Lanyon's and Jekyll's written accounts

questions.solution: The last two chapters are written documents that finally reveal the truth
questions.hint: Think about the titles of the last two chapters

questions.text: Whose theory of evolution made some Victorians fear that humans could become more primitive, a fear reflected in Hyde? Give the scientist's surname.
questions.solution: Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) unsettled ideas about human nature
questions.hint: He sailed round the world on HMS Beagle

questions.text: How does Stevenson suggest that respectable Victorian gentlemen hide secrets?

rubric.model_answer: Stevenson shows respectability as a mask. Jekyll is a wealthy, honoured doctor, yet he creates Hyde to indulge hidden desires without damaging his reputation. Utterson and Enfield agree never to mention the story of the door again, showing gentlemen avoided scandal rather than seeking the truth. Even the buildings reflect this: Jekyll's fine house faces a square, while the shabby laboratory door opens onto a back street. Jekyll admits man is 'not truly one, but truly two'.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: clear argument about secrecy and respectability
1 mark: Jekyll's double life and his motive
1 mark: Utterson and Enfield's silence
1 mark: setting or buildings as symbols (front and back doors)
1 mark: relevant quotation analysed
1 mark: Victorian context of reputation

questions.solution: Key ideas: Jekyll's double life, the gentlemen's agreement to stay silent, the two sides of Jekyll's house and Victorian respectability
questions.hint: Think about who keeps quiet, and why
